evidence.note: Every high-confidence story names a directly-opened tier-1 primary: the lead cites nvidianews.nvidia.com (the Huang and Altman quotes came from that page, not secondhand), Model Hypnosis cites the arXiv abstract, Firebird and Grok 4.6 cite blogs.nvidia.com and x.ai. The two stories resting on unconfirmed reporting are both capped at medium and say so in the copy — Anthropic's revenue ('The figures have not been confirmed by Anthropic on the record') and Stripe/OpenRouter ('neither company has publicly confirmed the price').

Vendor and single-origin claims are consistently framed as claims: 'Z.ai says it surfaced more than 2,400 vulnerabilities', 'according to Bloomberg, whose reporting was the basis for wider coverage'. Figures carry their basis — the Stripe multiple is given as '5.4 times the $1.3 billion valuation OpenRouter raised at in May' rather than a bare 'five times'.
Clean throughout; the Groq body's second paragraph still carries both the Nvidia licensing context and the antitrust-structuring aside in one long clause.

Stripe/OpenRouter was added on re-score after the classifier fix surfaced it — a $7bn acquisition is materially bigger than the $350m Groq round already running, and its absence was a real miss in the first pass. It runs at standard rather than top because the price traces to a single Bloomberg scoop that neither company has confirmed; prominence follows the sourcing, not the size of the number.

Policy sits at 0 against a target of 1 — see notes. Nvidia is a party in 3 of 10 stories, close to the rubric's one-third caution line, but each is a distinct event and edition.summary names Nvidia's centrality in its first sentence rather than burying it.

notes:
Re-scored from scratch after adding the Stripe/OpenRouter story; the eval-binding check in tools/validate.mjs correctly blocked publication on the stale 9-story binding, which is exactly the drift this mechanism exists to catch.

Policy is still empty against a quota target of 1 (minQuota is 0, so it does not block). This run is a partial vindication of the classifier fix and a clean example of the sourcing rule holding: the repaired classifier DID surface a genuine, in-window policy candidate the old one hid — WIRED's 14 Aug piece on state lawmakers drafting bills to bar human-AI marriage. It still does not run, because wired.com cannot be fetched by this pipeline and rule 1 is that a source which cannot be opened is not a source. The corroborating coverage that IS openable (Wisconsin's bill via WSAW, Ohio HB 469 via Fox News) dates to February 2026, far outside even the 480-hour maxLookback, so it cannot stand in for the fresh reporting. Correct outcome: no policy story.

Carried forward from the first pass, both still true and both now better evidenced: (1) input/sources.json has no dedicated policy-tracking outlet at tier 2 or better that this pipeline can actually open — Politico or a law-firm regulation tracker would raise the hit rate, and WIRED being unfetchable is a live example of the gap; (2) harvest.mjs's policy topic search returned nothing usable today, so policy research still depends on live WebSearch rather than the harvested pool the other beats draw from.
